title: A Talk for When You’re Tense
summary: Let tension go, one part at a time: to tense, to release.
script:
Take a moment now, just for yourself.

Settle into whatever position feels right for you today. Sitting, lying down, it doesn't matter, as long as your body feels held and comfortable.

Let your eyes close, softly, or rest gently downward if that feels better.

For the next few minutes, nothing needs your attention except this. Just you, and this quiet space you've made.

Feel the weight of your body against the surface beneath you. Notice how it holds you completely. Let your hands rest. Let your shoulders soften.

Take a slow breath in… and let it go.

Once more. Breathe in… breathe out.

Let your breath find its own natural pace, slow and unhurried, needing nothing from you but your attention.

Today, we're going to work with two simple actions, actions your body already knows how to do.

The first is to tense. To tense means to make your muscles hard because you are nervous, scared or stressed.

The second is to release. To release means let your muscles relax, completely, all at once, like opening a hand that was closed.

We'll move slowly through the body, tensing one part at a time, then releasing. Tense… and release. There's no need to rush. Each part deserves its own quiet attention.

Start with your hands. Make two fists. Squeeze tightly. Feel the tension building in your fingers, your palms, your wrists.

Hold it for a moment longer.

Now release. Let your hands open completely. Let your fingers fall soft and loose.

Notice the difference. Notice how much lighter your hands feel now, compared to a moment ago. This lightness has always been available to you.

Move to your arms. Bend your elbows slightly, and tense them. Make them firm, from your upper arms down to your wrists.

Hold that tension.

And release. Let your arms fall heavy, resting completely, doing nothing at all.

Notice this feeling. This is what relaxation feels like, right after tension leaves. A kind of softness that spreads quietly outward.

Bring your attention to your shoulders. Lift them towards your ears, and tense them there, firm and tight.

Hold it.

And release. Let them drop, far from your ears, completely loose.

Feel your shoulders sink a little deeper into stillness, as if they're settling into the surface beneath you.

Move to your face. Tense it gently. Close your eyes tightly, press your lips together, tighten your jaw.

Hold for this moment.

And release. Let your whole face go soft. Let your jaw drop slightly. Let your eyes rest, heavy and calm.

Notice how quickly the tension disappeared, once you let it go. Tension often needs less effort to release than we imagine.

Bring your attention to your stomach. Tense it, pulling it in slightly, making it firm.

Hold it there.

And release. Let it soften completely, rising and falling gently with your breath, as if it never held any tightness at all.

Now your legs. Straighten them slightly, and tense the muscles there, from your thighs down to your feet.

Hold this tension for a few seconds.

And release. Let your legs fall heavy, sinking into the surface beneath you, completely supported.

Take a slow breath here, noticing how much of your body has already softened. Notice how one release seems to lead gently into the next.

Finally, tense your whole body, all at once. Every muscle, from your head to your feet. Your hands, to your arms, your shoulders, your face, your stomach, your legs. Hold everything tight, just for a moment.

And now, release everything. All at once. Let your entire body go completely soft.

Notice this feeling spreading through you, like a wave moving slowly from your head down to your feet. This deep, complete release.

Tension always passes. It rises, and it falls, the same way your breath rises and falls. You don't need to fight it. You only need to notice it, and then, let it go.

Stay here for a while, simply feeling this stillness. No more tensing. Only release. Only rest.

Let these gentle words settle into your mind.

I release what I no longer need.

My body knows how to let it go.

I am calm.

I am safe.

I am completely at rest.

Take another slow breath, and let these words become part of you.

For a little while longer, just stay here. There's no rush to leave this feeling. Let your body remain heavy, loose, and quiet, for as long as it needs. Let your mind rest in this same stillness, without needing to think, or plan, or hold onto anything at all.

Notice how peaceful it is to simply be, without effort, without tension, without needing to be anywhere else.

When your mind feels ready, start to notice small things around you. The temperature of the air. Any distant sounds. The rhythm of your own breath, still slow and steady.

Let your fingers move first, just slightly. Then your feet. Small movements, waking up gently, without rushing this transition.

Take your time opening your eyes. There's no hurry. Let the calm you found stay with you as your eyes slowly adjust to the light around you.

Whatever you carry from this moment, let it be this: your body knows how to release. It always has. And it always will. Anytime tension returns, you can come back to this simple rhythm, tense, and release, and find this same stillness waiting for you.

vocabulary.definition: to make your muscles tight or hard, often because you feel nervous, scared, or stressed
to let the tension go and allow your muscles to relax completely, like opening a hand that was tightly closed

exercises.sentence: When I feel nervous, I tend _____ my shoulders, making them tight.
After holding my fists closed, I try _____ the tension and let my hands soften.
To make a muscle firm and tight, you need _____ it.
As I let my shoulders drop and relax, I begin _____ the tension.
